coredata.dc:description: A polyester polyurethane (PU)-degrading enzyme, PU esterase, derived from Pseudomonas fluorescens, a bacterium that utilizes polyester PU as the sole carbon source,was purified to homogeneity as indicated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gelelectrophoresis. This enzyme was a soluble, extracellular protein with a molecular mass of 48 kDa and was inhibited by phenylmethylsulfonylfluoride (PMSF). A genomic library of Ps.fluorescens was constructed using the Escherichia coli bacteriophage l vector lZAPII. A recombinant phage exhibiting activity against Impranil DLN was isolated. The geneencoding the polyurethanase (PUase) protein was subcloned into a plasmid expression vectorpT7-6 and expressed in E. coli. Upon expression, the PUase was secreted by the host,displayed esterase activity which was inhibited by PMSF, and in vivo 35S-methionine labeling of the gene product encoded by the open reading frame of the clone insertrevealed a single polypeptide with a molecular mass of 48 kDa.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: A polyester polyurethane (PU)-degrading enzyme, PU esterase, derived from Pseudomonas fluorescens, a bacterium that utilizes polyester PU as the sole carbon source,was purified to homogeneity as indicated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gelelectrophoresis. This enzyme was a soluble, extracellular protein with a molecular mass of 48 kDa and was inhibited by phenylmethylsulfonylfluoride (PMSF). A genomic library of Ps.fluorescens was constructed using the Escherichia coli bacteriophage l vector lZAPII. A recombinant phage exhibiting activity against Impranil DLN was isolated. The geneencoding the polyurethanase (PUase) protein was subcloned into a plasmid expression vectorpT7-6 and expressed in E. coli. Upon expression, the PUase was secreted by the host,displayed esterase activity which was inhibited by PMSF, and in vivo 35S-methionine labeling of the gene product encoded by the open reading frame of the clone insertrevealed a single polypeptide with a molecular mass of 48 kDa.

ce:section.ce:para: Polyurethanes (PUs) are a class of plastics which are widely used as raw materials in variousindustries. PUs are synthesized from polyols and polyisocyanates and are classified into two types,polyester PUs and polyether PUs. Polyester PUs are considered to be comparatively susceptible tomicrobial degradation (Morton and Surman, 1994). Despite its xenobiotic origins, PU hasbeen found to be susceptible to biodegradation by naturally occurring microorganisms (Pathirana and Seal, 1984; Bentham et al., 1987; Kay et al., 1991). Enzymatic attackon PUs could be contributed by hydrolases such as ureases attacking the urea bonds, proteasesattacking the amide bonds, and esterases attacking the many ester bonds (Evans and Levisohn, 1968; Hole, 1972; Flip, 1978; Griffin, 1980).

Several reports have appeared in the literature on the susceptibility of PUs to fungal attack.Mechanisms for this susceptibility have been suggested by Darby and Kaplan (1968)and Kaplan et al. (1968), who have shown that polyester-type PUs are more susceptible to fungalattack than other forms. Four species of fungi, Curvularia sengalensis, Fusarium solani, Aureobasidium pullulans and Cladosporium sp. were isolated by Crabbe et al., 1994with the capability of degrading an ester-based PU (ImpranilTMDLN). C. sengalensis was found to secrete an extracellular enzyme (molecular mass of 28 kDa) with esterase properties.

Kay et al., 1993reported on the degradation of solid PU by a Corynebacterium sp. In this study, an esterase activity was observed, however its relationship to PU degradationwas not established. Previously, a strain of Comamonas acidovorans was shown to utilizea solid polyester PU as the sole carbon and energy source (Nakajima-Kambe et al., 1997).In addition, it was shown that a cell-bound esterase played an important role in the degradation ofthe solid PU blocks (Akutsu et al., 1998). Previously, we reported the purification of a 29 kDa PU degrading protease from Pseudomonas fluorescens (Howard and Blake, 1998). This report describes the purification and characterization of an additional PU degradingenzyme from Ps. fluorescens and the cloning and expression of the gene in Escherichiacoli.

Bacterial strains used in this study were, except as noted, from the culture collection of theDepartment of Biological Sciences, Southeastern Louisiana University. The growth conditions forP. fluorescens were as previously reported (Howard and Blake, 1998. Escherichia coli strains XL1-Blue, C600, and DH5a were grown at 37°C in Luria–Bertani (LB)broth [1% (wt vol−1) bacto tryptone, 0.5% (wt vol−1) yeast extract, and1% (wt vol−1) NaCl]. For E. coli XL1-Blue infection with the bacteriophagelZAP II, cells were grown in LB broth supplemented with 10 mM MgSO4·7H2O and 0.2% (wt vol−1) maltose. For plasmid excision and rescue from lZAP II, infectedXL1-Blue cells were grown in 2X YT broth [1.6% (wt vol−1) bacto tryptone, 1% (wt vol−1) yeast extract and 1% (wt vol−1) NaCl]. When needed, ampicillin (100 mg ml−1) and/or kanamycin (80 mg ml−1) were added to themedium.

A 3 l culture of P. fluorescens was incubated for three days at 30°C with constantshaking (180 rpm) in yeast extract salts (YES) medium supplemented with (3.0 g l−1)Impranil DLN. At the end of the incubation period, little visible polyurethane remained. The culturesolids were removed by centrifugation at 10,000×g for 20 min at 4°C. All remainingmanipulations were also conducted at this temperature. The culture supernatant was concentrated3-fold by ultrafiltration on a minitan high-resolution tangential flow system fitted with a 10,000molecular weight cut-off membrane (Millipore). (NH4)2SO4 wasadded to the supernatant to give 60% saturation. The precipitated proteins were collected bycentrifugation (10,000×g for 15 min) and suspended in 50 mM phosphate buffer, pH 7.0and dialyzed in 4 l of the same solution overnight. The crude protein preparation was passed overa 5×7 cm column of DEAE–cellulose which had been previously equilibrated in 50 mM phosphatebuffer at pH 7.0 at a flow rate of ∼250 ml h−1. The non-binding fraction wasconcentrated by membrane filtration on a 10 kDa molecular weight cutoff (MWCO) membrane.

Non-denaturing (ND) polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) was run with a 12%polyacrylamide resolving gel as described by Calza et al. (1985). Sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS)–PAGE was performed as described by Laemmli (1970)with a 12% polyacrylamideresolving gel. Proteins were visualized by Coomassie blue staining.

During the purification, aliquots of the protein fractions were spotted on YES agar platessupplemented with Impranil at pH 6.8 and examined for zones of clearing at 30°C. Assays todetermine the proteolytic activity of the enzyme used hide powder azure in 50 mM phosphate bufferat pH 6.8 (Chavira et al., 1984). Activity against hide powder azure was determined bymonitoring the increase in absorbance at 595 nm. One unit of activity was defined as the amount ofenzyme that changes the absorbance at 595 nm by 0.01 min−1. In addition, the enzymewas assayed for esterase activity by its ability to release r-nitrophenol from 8 mMr-nitrophenylacetate in 50 mM phosphate buffer, pH 6.8 at 30°C (Deshpande et al., 1984).One unit of esterase activity was defined as the amount of enzyme that produced 1 mmole ofr-nitrophenol per min. All enzyme assays were observed to be linear with respect to time and proteinconcentration under the tested conditions.
Protein concentrations were estimated by the method of Kalb and Bernlohr (1977).

Chromosomal DNA was isolated from a 500 ml mid-log-phase culture of P. fluorescens by the method of Marmur (1961). The genomic DNA of P. fluorescens wasdigested with EcoRI. The 4–10 kb DNA fragments were excised from agarose gel andelectroeluted into dialysis tubing. The size-fractionated DNA (1 mg) was ligated with T4 DNAligase to the E. coli bacteriophage vector lZAP II (1 mg) which was pre-digested with EcoRI and alkaline phosphatase-treated. The resulting ligation mixture was head packaged in vitro (GigapackIII Gold, Stratagene) and used to infect E. coli XL1-Blue.Recombinant phage were screened for PUase activity by plating in LB soft agar, 0.7%, overlayscontaining 0.5% (vol vol−1) Impranil DLN. PUase positive recombinant phage wereidentified as plaques containing a zone of clearing around them.
Plasmid DNA was isolated by the alkaline lysis method as described by Sambrook et al. (1989).

Hybridizations were performed with the ECL direct nucleic acid labeling and detection system (Amersham Life Sciences). Hybridizations were carried out overnight at 42°C with 50% formamideand 6× SSC as suggested by the manufactures specifications. Membranes were washed for 30 minwith 0.1× SSC/0.1% SDS at 42°C prior to autoradiography.

A 3.4 kb SalI–EcoRI DNA fragment of pREV1 was cloned into theexpression vectors pT7-5 and pT7-6 (Tabor and Richardson, 1985). Protein expression andlabeling with 35S methionine was performed according to the protocol described by Tabor, 1990.

The l phage library of P. fluorescens contained approximately 7,537 recombinantphage with insert sizes ranging from 4–10 kb. The recombinant phage were screened for hydrolysisof Impranil DLN and 8 clones coding for PUase activity were detected. However, from the restrictionpatterns of the PUase positive clones in lZAP II, the eight PUase clones were determined to be thesame. Thus, one PUase positive clone (pREV1) was retained for further analysis (Fig. 1 ).

Restriction mapping of pREV1 showed that the clone contained a recombinant insert of 5.5 kb (Fig. 2 ). The insert was cleaved by six of the restriction enzymes tested. A single restriction site was foundfor ClaI, HindIII, AccI, SalI, SmaI, and BamHIand two sites for KpnI. No sites were located for the restriction enzymes PstI, XbaI, XhoI, NotI, EcoRV, PvuI and BglII.

To ensure that the gene of pREV1 was from P. fluorescens, P. fluorescenschromosomal DNA and pREV1 DNA were analyzed by Southern hybridization (Fig. 3 ). The labeled EcoRI fragment from pREV1 was used as the probe. Under the stringencyconditions used, the probe hybridized to a 5.5 kb DNA fragment from the P. fluorescensgenomic DNA cut with EcoRI and this fragment comigrated with the 5.5 kb DNA fragmentfrom the EcoRI cut pREV1 DNA. These results indicate that pREV1 originated from thechromosomal DNA of P. fluorescens and is a single copy per chromosome.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Phenotypic expression of pREV1 in E. coli
ce:section.ce:para: Subcloning of DNA fragments from pREV1 was performed to localize the polyurethanasegene contained within the 5.5 kb EcoRI insert. Upon subcloning of the 3.4 kb SalI–EcoRI fragment, polyurethanase activity was observed as noted by a zone of clearingaround the recombinant colonies. However, subcloning of the 2.3 kb BamHI–EcoRI fragment led to the loss of polyurethanse activity.

The phenotype of the recombinant pREV1 was analyzed for the gene product encoded by in vivo transcription/translation analysis. The 3.4 kb SalI–EcoRI DNAfragment of pREV1 was subcloned into the expression vectors pT7-5 and pT7-6. The resultingsubclones, pEX5 and pEX6, were electroporated into E. coli C600 containing the pGP1-2.This expression system revealed one 35S-methionine labeled polypeptide which wasencoded by pEX6. The relative molecular weight of this polypeptide was estimated to be 48 kDa (Fig. 4 ). No 35S-methionine labeled polypeptides were observed in the pEX5 clone. Theseresults indicated that the opening reading frame (ORF) of pEX6 is in the correct orientation to betranscribed by the T7 promoter.

A summary of the purification of a 48 kDa polyurethanase protein from P. fluorescens is described in Table 1 . Protein concentrations were estimated by the method of Kalb and Bernlohr (1977), sincethe concentration of proteins was below detectable limits of sensitivity for the method of Bradford (1976). The steps of the purification were completed in <10 h and resulted in 2.6%recovery of enzymatic activity in the cell-free extract. The approximate molecular mass of the PUaseprotein was estimated to be 48 kDa as compared to the SDS–PAGE molecular weight standards Fig. 6.

The catalytic properties of the purified protein revealed an esterase activity. Usingr-nitrophenylacetate (rNPAc) as the esterase substrate, the purified protein displayed a specificactivity of 7.6 U mg−1. In addition, the enzyme exhibited activity againstr-nitrophenylpropionate (rNPP), 6.7 U mg−1. The optimum pH for the enzyme activitytowards r-nitrophenylacetate was determined to be 7.0. The enzyme activity was stable after 10 minat 100°C, and the esterase activity was inhibited 51% by the addition of 1 mM PMSF. When hidepowder azure, a known trypsin substrate, was used as the protease substrate, the purified proteindisplayed no activity against this substrate, indicating that the enzyme exhibited only esterase activityand displayed no protease activity.

The use of phage l as a cloning vector in this study enabled the cloning of large fragments ofP. fluorescens DNA. In this study, we identified a single unique PUase gene. The library intheory (average insert size approx. 7 kb) was large enough to represent the entire chromosomeseveral times, however the 29 kDa PUase purified previously (Howard and Blake, 1998) wasnot obtained. The failure to isolate this PUase gene might be due to the restriction endonuclease EcoRI, used to generate the library, cleaving the gene such that phenotypic expression is notobserved or the gene is contained on a larger (>10 kb) EcoRI DNA fragment.

This is the first published report on the cloning of a PUase gene from P. fluorescens.The PUase encoded by pREV1 is similar to the PUase enzyme purified from P. fluorescensin this study. The cloned and native PUase proteins have not yet been sequenced. However, they bothshow similar activity which strongly suggest their identity. The esterase activity and inhibition withPMSF of E. coli pREV1 is consistent with that of the purified PUase. Likewise, themolecular weight of the gene product from pEX6 (48 kDa) is the same as that of the purified nativePUase protein.

Our laboratory has also cloned and sequenced a 65 kDa PUase from P. chlororaphis (unpublished data). DNA sequencing analysis revealed that the deduced amino acid sequence for theORF contained a typical serine–protease motif, GXSXG, as the catalytic site. In addition, the aminoacid sequence has high similiarity with several lipase proteins.

We are presently in the process of subjecting pREV1 to DNA sequencing analysis. Theseresults will yield valuable information about the structure/function of the enzyme as well as regulationof the gene. We are also in the process of constructing another l phage library for P. fluorescens in attempt of obtaining the 29 kDa protease gene.

The purification of the PUase from P. fluorescens resulted in a low recovery ofenzyme activity (2.6%). The low yield of enzyme activity recovery was also noted in the purificationof a 31 kDa PUase from P. chlororaphis, 5%, (Ruiz et al., 1999). The substrateused in these assays was rNPAc, a general esterase substrate. Other esterase enzymes are probablypresent in the culture supernatant resulting in the overall esterase activity. However, the purificationof the PUase enzyme was monitored by the observation of zones of clearing in radial diffusion assayson PU agar plates. Thus, the PUase could account for only a small portion of the total esteraseactivity found in the extracellular protein fraction. Consequently, the 48 kDa esterase could havebeen degraded by proteolysis resulting in lower enzyme activity. The purification of the 48 kDaesterase (this study) and the 29 kDa protease (Howard and Blake, in press) are similar however,the two proteins are fractionated by anion exchange chromatography. The presence of the proteolyticenzyme could contribute to the degradation of the esterase protein. This proteolytic cleavage of theesterase protein may explain the minor protein bands as observed in the SDS–PAGE Fig. 6.

The chemical, physical, and enzymatic characteristics of the purified PUase from P.fluorescens as well as the inhibition by PMSF suggest that this PUase is similar to other PUasespreviously described. The esterase activity and inhibition of enzyme activity by PMSF of the proteinfrom this study is consistent with that of the PUase purified from C. sengalensis (Crabbe et al., 1994), the two PUases from Ps. chlororaphis (Ruiz et al., 1999),and the two PUases from C. acidovorans (Allen et al., 1999; Akutsu et al., 1998). However, there are some differences among these PUases. The PUase from C.sengalensis has a molecular weight of 28 kDa (Crabbe et al., 1994), whereas one PUasefrom P. chlororaphis has a molecular weight of 65 kDa while the other PUase has amolecular weight of 31 kDa (Ruiz et al., 1999). One of the PUase proteins from C.acidovorans has a molecular weight of 62 kDa (Akutsu et al., 1998), while anotherPUase has a molecular weight of 45 kDa and also displays protease activity (Allen et al., 1999). In addition, a second PUase from P. fluorescens was shown to have a molecularweight of 29 kDa (Howard and Blake, in Press), displayed protease activity, and was also inhibitedby PMSF. Thus, all the PUase enzymes described thus far are inhibited by PMSF, indicating that theseproteins which are involved in PU degradation have a serine-type protease motif in the catalytic site.
